rv.q: Hwang is among the great writers of big ideas currently working on the American stage.
The play retains its bite in part because its essential subject, like that of many a good comedy, is human folly.
David Henry Hwang and Yellow Face get the well-deserved last laughs.

Those questions, both as artistic choices and as problems of social identity, are powerfully and hilariously engaged in the revival of David Henry Hwang’s “Yellow Face” that opened on Tuesday at the Theater.
Every chance Asian-American artists get to tell their own stories—even insular ones of foolishness and compromise—is a step to the future, face forward.
Weird as it may sound, "Yellow Face" is a good time in the company of smart, self-aware people, critical thinkers willing to ponder the lessons and the follies of the past.
Mr. Hwang has created a work that is both deeply personal and bracingly political.

The play has urgent social concerns that are right at home at a theater like the Public, where it runs through Oct. 27, but pat resolutions and a little too much window-dressing prevent the conflicts from becoming uncomfortably real.
Huang's script is a masterclass in threading the needle between comedy and drama.
Yellow Face is as thoughtful as it is playful, not the self-indulgent autobiography that DHH himself calls it in the play itself.
Hwang’s genius here is his ability to spin his real life into a fascinatingly entertaining work using all these events and characters.

Not everything in the play or production works perfectly, but “Yellow Face” never whitewashes a very important life lesson: Check your biases and misperceptions every single day before you take any action or open up your mouth.

There’s something touching is his removing the unseen mask—the imagined make-up he obviously never literally brushed on—that in this final Yellow Face development lifts the self-involved piece to a praise-worthy height.
Also because Hwang is so proudly flaunting his dramaturgical transgression.
Laughter plus discernment make for a hearty meal, even when the dessert comes first.
It is funny and messy, and not without its structural flaws. But the questions it asks of Hwang and the audience make it both a rollicking and thought-provoking evening.
Yellow Face pushes its conversation through its racially subversive, often cheeky casting choices in the ensemble.
And though its late turn into earnestness does not quite land in Leigh Silverman's tonally uneven staging, this revival is nonetheless thoughtful and tremendously entertaining.
Good Bones features meditations on wealth, class, identity, and belonging, accompanied by the sound of an unquiet spirit.
Yellow Face doesn’t fire on all cylinders but one can’t deny its relevance to contemporary concerns.
The strident tone, vapid observations and clunky structure, render this play as unfunny and not very interesting.
Provocative and clever, Yellow Face raises excellent questions on bias and perception, with particular attention to questions like “where are you really from?”

cn.t: Critics praise Hwang's sharp, funny meta-theatrical satire as bracingly relevant, with standout performances from Daniel Dae Kim. A few find it overly self-indulgent, but most laud its incisive take on race and representation.
